Consider the routing protocols given in List I and the names given in List II:

Suppose two hosts use a TCP connection to transfer a large file. Which of the following statements is/are FALSE with respect to the TCP connection?
I. If the sequence number of a segment is m, then the sequence number of the subsequent segment is always m+1.
II. If the estimated round trip time at any given point of time is t sec, the value of the retransmission timeout is always set to greater than or equal to t sec.
III. The size of the advertised window never changes during the course of the TCP connection.
IV. The number of unacknowledged bytes at the sender is always less than or equal to the advertised window.

- II: RTO is set to at least the estimated RTT [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True
- III: the advertised window changes as the receive buffer fills and empties [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False

questions.question:
Consider the following three statements about link state and distance vector routing protocols, for a large network with 500 network nodes and 4000 links
[S1] The computational overhead in link state protocols is higher than in distance vector protocols.
[S2] A distance vector protocol (with split horizon) avoids persistent routing loops, but not a link state protocol.
[S3] After a topology change, a link state protocol will converge faster than a distance vector protocol.
Which one of the following is correct about S1, S2, and S3?

options.A: S1, S2, and S3 are all true
options.B: S1, S2, and S3 are all false.
options.C: S1 and S2 are true, but S3 is false
options.D: S1 and S3 are true, but S2 is false.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- S1: each link-state router runs Dijkstra on the whole topology [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] more computation True
- S2: split horizon does not prevent all loops (count-to-infinity can still happen), while link-state avoids persistent loops False
- S3: link-state floods updates and recomputes at once [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] faster convergence True

Answer: S1 and S3 are true, but S2 is false

questions.question: TCP client P successfully establishes a connection to TCP server [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_P [/latex] denote the sequence number in the SYN sent from [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] to [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Let [latex]N_Q [/latex] denote the acknowledgement number in the SYN ACK from Q to P. Which of the following statements is/are CORRECT?

options.A: The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is chosen randomly by [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex]
options.B: The sequence number [latex]N_P [/latex] is always 0 for a new connection
options.C: The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P [/latex]
options.D: The acknowledgement number [latex]N_Q [/latex] is equal to [latex]N_P+1 [/latex]

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- The initial sequence number (ISN) is chosen randomly (to avoid confusion with old segments and for security) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE; it is not always 0.
- A SYN segment consumes one sequence number, so Q acknowledges with the next expected number: [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (so [latex]N_Q=N_P[/latex] is false).

Answer: [latex]N_P[/latex] is chosen randomly by P; [latex]N_Q=N_P+1[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider a new TCP connection between a sender and a receiver. The receiver advertised window is constant at [latex]48[/latex] KB, the maximum segment size (MSS) is [latex]2[/latex] KB, and the slow start threshold for TCP congestion control is [latex]16[/latex] KB. Assume that there are no timeouts or duplicate acknowledgements. The number of rounds of transmission required for the congestion control algorithm of the TCP connection to reach the congestion avoidance phase is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex]
questions.explanation:
In TCP slow start, [latex]\text{cwnd}[/latex] starts at [latex]1[/latex] MSS and doubles every round-trip, until it reaches the slow-start threshold ([latex]\text{ssthresh}=16[/latex] KB), at which point congestion avoidance begins.

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Round}&\text{cwnd}\\\hline1&2\text{ KB (1 MSS)}\\2&4\text{ KB}\\3&8\text{ KB}\\4&16\text{ KB}\end{array}[/latex]

At the end of round [latex]4[/latex], [latex]\text{cwnd}[/latex] reaches exactly [latex]16[/latex] KB, equal to [latex]\text{ssthresh}[/latex] — so it takes [latex]4[/latex] rounds of slow-start doubling before the connection is ready to switch into the congestion-avoidance phase.

Answer: 4

questions.question: Suppose a message of size 15000 bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. Each router has a defined maximum transmission unit (MTU) as shown in the figure, including IP header. The number of fragments that will be delivered to the destination is _________. (Answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
Assume the standard [latex]20[/latex]-byte IPv4 header (no options), so the original datagram is [latex]15000+20=15020[/latex] bytes.

At Router-1 (MTU [latex]5000[/latex]): max data per fragment [latex]=5000-20=4980[/latex] bytes, but fragment data must be a multiple of [latex]8[/latex] bytes, so usable data per (non-last) fragment [latex]=\lfloor4980/8\rfloor\times8=4976[/latex] bytes.
[latex]15000[/latex] bytes of data [latex]\div4976\approx3.01[/latex]: so [latex]3[/latex] full fragments of [latex]4976[/latex] bytes ([latex]14928[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]15000-14928=72[/latex] bytes. Total after Router-1: 4 fragments.

At Router-2 (MTU [latex]3000[/latex]): each fragment bigger than [latex]3000[/latex] bytes must be split again; the small [latex]72[/latex]-byte-data fragment (total size [latex]92[/latex] bytes) passes straight through unchanged.
Max data per new sub-fragment [latex]=3000-20=2980[/latex], rounded down to a multiple of [latex]8[/latex]: [latex]\lfloor2980/8\rfloor\times8=2976[/latex] bytes.
Each of the [latex]3[/latex] big fragments (data [latex]=4976[/latex] bytes) splits into: one sub-fragment of [latex]2976[/latex] bytes, plus a final sub-fragment of [latex]4976-2976=2000[/latex] bytes — [latex]2[/latex] sub-fragments each, so [latex]3\times2=6[/latex] sub-fragments total.

Total fragments reaching the destination [latex]=6[/latex] (from the split large fragments) [latex]+1[/latex] (the small fragment that passed through) [latex]=7[/latex].

Answer: 7

questions.question:
A TCP sender successfully establishes a connection with a TCP receiver and starts the transmission of segments. The TCP congestion control mechanism's slow-start threshold is set to [latex]10000[/latex] segments. Assume that the round-trip time is fixed at [latex]1[/latex] millisecond. Assume that the sender always has data to send, the segments are numbered from [latex]1[/latex], and no segment is lost. Let [latex]t[/latex] denote the time (in milliseconds) at which the transmission of segment number [latex]2000[/latex] starts.

Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation:
In slow start, the congestion window (in segments) doubles every RTT, starting from [latex]1[/latex] segment, as long as it stays below the threshold ([latex]10000[/latex], which is far above anything we'll reach here).

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{RTT (start time, ms)}&\text{cwnd (segments sent)}&\text{Segment numbers sent}\\\hline0&1&1\\1&2&2\text{-}3\\2&4&4\text{-}7\\3&8&8\text{-}15\\4&16&16\text{-}31\\5&32&32\text{-}63\\6&64&64\text{-}127\\7&128&128\text{-}255\\8&256&256\text{-}511\\9&512&512\text{-}1023\\10&1024&1024\text{-}2047\end{array}[/latex]

Segment number [latex]2000[/latex] falls in the batch sent starting at time [latex]t=10[/latex]ms (the [latex]1024[/latex]-[latex]2047[/latex] range).

Answer: [latex]10\le t<11[/latex]

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
A sender uses the Stop-and Wait ARQ protocol for reliable transmission of frames. Frames are of size 1000bytes and the transmission rate at the sender is 80Kbps(1Kbps=1000 bits/second). Size of anacknowledgement is 100bytes and the transmission rate at the receiver is 8Kbps. The one-way propagation delay is 100milliseconds.

- ACK transmission: 800 bits / 8 Kbps = 0.1 s
- Propagation: 0.1 s each way

One frame every 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 0.4 s [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] throughput = 1000 / 0.4 = 2500 bytes/s

Answer: 2500

questions.question: Consider a token ring network with a length of 2km having 10 stations including a monitoring station. Consider routing table of an organization's router shown below:
[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|} Subnet Number & Subnet Mask & Next Hop \\ 12.20.164.0 & 255.255.252.0 & R1 \\ 12.20.170.0 & 255.255.254.0 & R2 \\ 12.20.168.0 & 255.255.254.0 & Interface 0 \\ 12.20.166.0 & 255.255.254.0 & Interface 1 \\ default & ~ & R3 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

questions.question:
Consider a network with five nodes, N1 to N5, as shown below

The network uses a Distance Vector Routing protocol. Once the routes have stabilized, the distance vectors at different nodes are as following. N1: (0, 1, 7, 8, 4) N2: (1, 0, 6, 7, 3) N3: (7, 6, 0, 2, 6) N4: (8, 7, 2, 0, 4) N5: (4, 3, 6, 4, 0) Each distance vector is the distance of the best known path at the instance to nodes, N1 to N5, where the distance to itself is 0. Also, all links are symmetric and the cost is identical in both directions. In each round, all nodes exchange their distance vectors with their respective neighbors. Then all nodes update their distance vectors. In between two rounds, any change in cost of a link will cause the two incident nodes to change only that entry in their distance vectors.

The cost of link N2-N3 reduces to 2(in both directions). After the next round of updates, what will be the new distance vector at node, N3?
questions.explanation:
N3's neighbours are N2 (now cost 2) and N4 (cost 2). Vectors received:
N2 = (1, 0, 2, 7, 3), N4 = (8, 7, 2, 0, 4)

- to N1: min(2 + 1, 2 + 8) = 3
- to N2: 2, to N4: 2
- to N5: min(2 + 3, 2 + 4) = 5

New vector = (3, 2, 0, 2, 5)

Answer: (3, 2, 0, 2, 5)
